title: Intranasal oxytocin increases neural responses to social reward in post-traumatic stress disorder

what_it_measured.text: Future studies are needed to investigate clinical effects of oxytocin.
As a first step to investigate this therapeutical potential, we investigated whether intranasal oxytocin enhances neural sensitivity to social reward in PTSD patients.

dose.text: Under supervision of the experimenter participants selfadministered oxytocin (40 IU, Defiante Farmaceutica, S.A., Funchal Portugal) and placebo (0.8% NaCl solution) via nasal spray (10 puffs, 5 puffs per nostril).

route.text: Under supervision of the experimenter participants selfadministered oxytocin (40 IU, Defiante Farmaceutica, S.A., Funchal Portugal) and placebo (0.8% NaCl solution) via nasal spray (10 puffs, 5 puffs per nostril).

Within the PTSD and control group separately, correlations were assessed between CAPS symptom severity (PTSD group only), subjective ratings, neural responses in the placebo condition, and with the extent of the oxytocin effect (delta oxytocin-placebo).
RTs were assessed (milliseconds between start of target presentation and response).

reported_results.text: However, PTSD males reported more types of traumatic events during childhood compared with male controls, as assessed with the ETI (t(30.39) = −2.047, P = 0.049).
Under placebo, there was a significant main effect of sex on reward trial RT [F(1,68) = 11.295, P = 0.001], men being faster than women.
This group-difference in exposure to work-related traumatic events in females was no longer significant when controlling for years of police service (P > 0.1).

Oxytocin effect on subjective punishment ratings (delta OT-PL) was significantly negatively correlated to CAPS score (r = −0.464, P = 0.008), such that higher CAPS scores were related to a stronger dampening of punishment ratings after oxytocin compared with placebo.

Post hoc t-tests (see Supplementary Table S5) revealed that in PTSD patients, oxytocin significantly increased reward responses compared to placebo within the right putamen [t(34) = −2.927, P = 0.006] and left AI [t(34) = −2.234, P = 0.032], whereas in controls, oxytocin significantly decreased reward responses compared with placebo in the putamen [t(36) = 2.207, P = 0.034] and AI [t(36) = 2.879, P = 0.007] (Figure 3B and D).
Error bars indicate standard error of the mean. *P < 0.05.
